2048.heroParagraph: 2048 was created by Italian developer Gabriele Cirulli in March 2014 as an open-source clone of the tile-merging game Threes. This build runs on a fixed 4x4 grid and includes a built-in AI: press the Auto-run button and the game's own heuristic solver (which scores boards on tile smoothness, monotonic ordering, and open-cell count) takes over the arrow keys for you.
instructions: Use the arrow keys to slide every tile on the board in that direction at once; two tiles with the same number merge into one tile with double the value the instant they collide, and after every move the game drops a new tile into a random empty cell — 90% of the time a 2, 10% of the time a 4.
The game is won the moment any tile reaches the value 2048, but the board keeps accepting moves afterward if you want to keep merging toward higher tiles once that condition is met.

Press the Auto-run button to hand control to the built-in solver, which picks each move by evaluating board smoothness and monotonicity rather than playing randomly — watching a few of its moves is a fast way to see why keeping your highest tile in a corner matters.

sections.heading: Keep your highest tile cornered
sections.body: Because every arrow-key move slides the entire board in one direction, a high-value tile that is not pinned in a corner gets shuffled around and blocks merges instead of anchoring them. Picking one corner and repeatedly sliding toward it keeps your largest tiles stacked in descending order along that edge.

sections.heading: Watch the 90/10 spawn odds
sections.body: New tiles spawn as a 2 nine times out of ten and a 4 the rest of the time, always in an empty cell. Since you cannot control where the new tile lands, leaving at least one empty row or column gives the spawn room to land without immediately blocking your next planned merge.

sections.heading: Avoid sliding toward your empty side
sections.body: The board only fills up once open cells run out, so repeatedly sliding in the direction that empties tiles away from your corner strategy is what causes most losses — once movesAvailable() returns false because every adjacent tile has a different value, the run ends immediately.

rooftopsnipers.heroParagraph: Rooftop Snipers comes from New Eich Games, the studio also behind Getaway Shootout and House of Hazards. Two ragdoll gunmen face off on a narrow rooftop, and a single well-placed shot sends the loser flying off the edge — there is no health bar, just knockback and gravity.

Since a single hit can knock a ragdoll clean off the rooftop, jumping at the wrong moment can put you directly in your opponent's line of fire — timing a jump to close distance while your opponent is mid-recoil from their own shot is safer than jumping into an open lane.

The rooftop has a finite width, so being knocked backward near the edge ends the round even from a shot that would only stagger a player standing at center stage; controlling your on-screen position matters as much as landing hits.

sections.heading: Holding the shoot key aims, tapping it doesn't
sections.body: A quick tap fires immediately at whatever angle the rifle is already at, while holding the key raises it and lets you adjust before releasing. Against an opponent who is jumping, holding briefly to track their arc before firing lands more shots than tapping on reflex.

sections.heading: Position matters more than accuracy alone
sections.body: Because the rooftop has hard edges, a hit near the edge ends the round even if the same shot would only stagger a player standing at center. Retreating toward the middle after landing a hit, rather than pressing the advantage right at the edge, avoids letting one lucky return shot end the round instantly.

sections.heading: Jumping opens you up mid-air
sections.body: Jumping to close distance puts your character in a predictable arc with no way to change direction until landing, so jumping while your opponent still has a clear shot is one of the most common ways to lose a round. Jumping right after your opponent fires, while they are still in recoil, is safer than jumping on an open lane.

Hazards like the swinging hammer or the toaster's flying toast trigger automatically as players walk near them and will hit whoever is closest regardless of which player caused it, so a hazard that just fired is briefly safer to walk past than one that hasn't triggered yet.

sections.heading: Crouching dodges more than jumping does

sections.heading: Hazards reset on a timer, not on demand
sections.body: A hazard that just triggered needs a moment before it can fire again, so the instant after a hammer swings or toast launches is the safest window to walk past that specific spot. Waiting out an active hazard's reset is usually faster than detouring around it.

sections.heading: Race the task, not the other player
sections.body: Since completing your assigned task is what scores points, chasing down an opponent to block them costs time you could spend finishing your own task, especially in 1-player mode against computer opponents that path directly to their goal without hesitation.

drivemad.heroParagraph: Drive Mad is a physics driving game built around just two controls — accelerate and brake — spread across roughly 100 browser levels. The car's suspension behaves like a ragdoll: accelerating tips the body forward, braking tips it backward, and both actions have visible, sometimes exaggerated consequences on the vehicle's balance.
instructions: Hold the accelerate key to move forward and tip the car's weight forward, and hold the brake key to slow down and tip the weight backward — there is no steering input, so every obstacle is solved through throttle and brake timing alone, not lateral movement.

The first ten to fifteen levels are built to teach this balance-and-timing rhythm on relatively forgiving terrain; difficulty ramps up sharply afterward, so a technique that works on an early icy slope may fail on a later level that changes the vehicle entirely.

Surfaces change how the car behaves from level to level: wooden bridges bounce under the car's weight, ramps launch it higher than a flat surface would, and some levels reverse which key accelerates versus brakes, so read each new level's terrain before committing to a throttle rhythm that worked on the last one.

sections.heading: Balance is the whole game, not steering
sections.body: With only accelerate and brake as inputs, tipping the car too far forward or backward is what causes most crashes, not misjudging distance. Tapping the throttle in short bursts rather than holding it down keeps the car's body closer to level on uneven terrain like ramps or bridges.

sections.heading: Different vehicles behave completely differently
sections.body: The vehicle changes across levels — a stretch limo handles nothing like a rocket-propelled car — so the same tap rhythm that cleared one level can immediately fail on the next. Treat each new vehicle's first obstacle as a calibration test for how sensitive its balance is before committing to full-speed inputs.

sections.heading: Surface changes momentum without warning
sections.body: Wooden bridges bounce, ramps add unexpected height, and ice removes traction almost entirely, all without any on-screen indicator before you reach them. Slowing down slightly on approach to any new surface type gives more room to correct if the car reacts differently than the previous stretch of road.

retrobowl.heroParagraph: Retro Bowl was built by New Star Games, the British studio founded by Simon Read that also made New Star Soccer, and released in January 2020. Off the field, contract negotiations, player morale, and coaching staff upgrades all draw from the same limited salary cap, so a big free-agent signing at quarterback can leave no budget left to replace an aging offensive line.

Swipe down to call a timeout when a drive stalls or the play clock is about to run out; timeouts are limited per half, so saving at least one for a late defensive stop matters more than using it to reset an early third down.

sections.heading: Reading the pocket before you move

sections.heading: Bullet passes trade accuracy for speed
sections.body: A double-tap bullet pass gets the ball to a receiver faster, which matters against tight coverage, but it is less forgiving of a mistimed throw than a normal swipe pass. Save bullet passes for receivers who are clearly open rather than using them as a default.

sections.heading: The salary cap connects every decision
sections.body: Retro Bowl ties contract offers, coaching upgrades, and player morale to one shared budget, so overspending to keep a star receiver can quietly weaken the rest of the roster for seasons afterward. Press up while touching a wall to wall-jump off it; leaping toward a wall and pressing jump again the instant you touch it kicks you off in the opposite direction, and stringing several wall jumps together is how vertical shafts and wide gaps get crossed.

buildnow-gg.heroParagraph: BuildNow GG was released by battlelab in August 2021, combining building and gunplay into fast 1v1 duels: land in the arena, break objects for starting materials, and use walls and ramps for cover the instant an opponent comes into view.
instructions: Move with WASD, jump with Space, shoot with left-click, and aim down sights with right-click; the loadout — pistol, machine gun, sniper rifle, shotgun, and pickaxe — carries unlimited ammo on every weapon, so conserving ammunition is never a concern the way material conservation is.

Break crates and scenery with the pickaxe to gather building material before an opponent is spotted, since scrambling to gather material after a fight has already started leaves you without cover when it matters most.

The instant an opponent appears, building a defensive box gives cover to peek and shoot from — editing a window into a wall to fire through, rather than fully exposing yourself over the top, keeps most of your body protected while still landing shots.

sections.heading: Gather material before you need it
sections.body: Because building material only comes from breaking objects in the arena, waiting until an enemy is already visible to start collecting leaves no time to construct real cover. A quick sweep of nearby breakables right after landing pays off the moment a fight starts.

sections.heading: Edited windows beat exposed peeking
sections.body: Editing a wall to open a window-sized gap lets you return fire while keeping most of your box intact, which protects more of your body than peeking fully over an unedited wall. This matters most against the sniper rifle, where a single exposed shot can end the fight.

sections.heading: Unlimited ammo removes one kind of resource management, not all of it
sections.body: Since every weapon has unlimited ammo, the only resource actually worth managing is building material and health — spraying freely with the machine gun costs nothing directly, but the time spent missing shots is time an opponent can use to build height or reposition.

sections.heading: Manual clicking has a hard ceiling
sections.body: Since each click earns exactly one Dogecoin regardless of how the game has progressed, clicking never scales the way helper-based income does — the practical value of clicking drops sharply once even a few helpers are generating passive income each second.

sections.heading: Reinvest early rather than banking coins
sections.body: Because helper income compounds over time (more helpers means more coins per second, which buys more helpers faster), spending Dogecoin on helpers as soon as they are affordable outpaces saving up coins for a single larger purchase later.

sections.heading: The moon is a long-term goal, not a quick one
sections.body: The game's stated goal of reaching the moon requires substantial passive income built up over an extended session, so treating early clicking and helper purchases as a warm-up phase rather than the main event matches how the game's progression is actually paced.

duckhunt.heroParagraph: This build is a Flash-era browser recreation of the Duck Hunt light-gun concept popularized by Nintendo's 1984 arcade release, running through the Ruffle Flash emulator since native Flash support was discontinued. Ducks fly across the screen in short, unpredictable bursts, and each wave has a limited number of shots before it ends.
instructions: Move the mouse to aim your crosshair and click to fire; unlike a keyboard-only shooter, aim is entirely analog through mouse position rather than snapping to discrete lanes or targets.

Press R to reload once your shots for the current wave run out — missing shots still counts against your limited ammo, so firing at a duck that has already changed direction wastes a shot that a wave often cannot afford to lose.

Press Space to start the next wave once the current one clears; ducks tend to move faster and change direction more abruptly as waves progress, so a shot pattern that worked on an early wave may not track a later wave's movement.

sections.heading: Lead the duck, don't chase it
sections.body: Because ducks change direction abruptly and the crosshair takes a moment to move with the mouse, clicking where a duck currently is often fires behind where it has already moved. Aiming slightly ahead of a duck's flight path lands more hits than tracking its exact current position.

sections.heading: Ammo is limited per wave, not per shot
sections.body: Since each wave gives a fixed number of shots before requiring a reload, missing early in a wave leaves fewer shots to clear the remaining ducks. Waiting half a second for a clean, close shot is usually worth more than firing early at a duck still far away or moving unpredictably.

sections.heading: Later waves need a faster aim update, not just faster clicking
sections.body: As waves progress, ducks move faster and change direction more abruptly, so the skill that scales is how quickly the aim adjusts to a duck's new heading, not how quickly the mouse button is clicked. A rushed shot on a wrong prediction wastes ammo that a later, corrected shot could have used instead.

bejeweled2.metaKeywords: Bejeweled 2, bejeweled 2 unblocked, popcap games, match 3 puzzle, flame gem hypercube, schplay bejeweled 2
bejeweled2.heroParagraph: Bejeweled 2 is PopCap Games' 2004 sequel to the original Bejeweled, adding special gems created by matching more than the minimum three: a four-gem match creates a Flame Gem, a five-in-a-row creates a Hypercube, and two matches intersecting in a T, L, or plus shape creates a Star Gem, each triggering a different clearing effect when detonated.
instructions: Click one gem, then click an adjacent gem to swap them; a swap that creates a horizontal or vertical match of three or more clears those gems, while a swap that creates no match reverses itself automatically.

Matching exactly four gems of the same color creates a Flame Gem that, when later matched, clears every gem in a 3x3 area around it, including triggering any other special gems caught in that blast radius.

Matching five gems in a row creates a Hypercube; swapping a Hypercube with any regular gem clears every gem of that gem's color from the entire board, making it the most valuable special gem to save for a color that has spread widely across the grid.

sections.heading: Star Gems come from intersections, not straight lines
sections.body: Unlike Flame Gems and Hypercubes, a Star Gem requires two matches crossing each other in a T, L, or plus shape rather than a longer straight line. When detonated, it clears its entire row and column plus triggers any special gems caught in that cross, making it useful for cutting through a cluttered board.

sections.heading: Save Hypercubes for spread-out colors
sections.body: Because a Hypercube clears every gem of whatever color it is swapped into, it delivers the most value when that color has spread across many separate clusters on the board rather than already being grouped into an easy match — using one on a color that was about to match normally anyway wastes its potential.

sections.heading: Chain reactions multiply special-gem value
sections.body: Detonating a Flame Gem or Star Gem near another special gem triggers both at once, and the gems that fall to refill the board can themselves complete new matches. Planning a match near an existing special gem, rather than in an empty part of the board, increases the odds of a chain reaction that clears far more than one match alone.

learntofly.heroParagraph: Learn to Fly was released by Light Bringer Games and casts a penguin trying to prove flightless birds can fly, sliding down a ramp and gliding as far as possible over open water. Distance earns coins, which fund permanent upgrades between attempts to slide, glide, and eventually rocket farther than the last run.
instructions: Use the left and right arrow keys to tilt the penguin's glide angle in flight — tilting back raises the nose for lift at the cost of speed, while tilting forward trades altitude for speed; the game can also be switched to mouse-steering in the options menu.

Once rockets are purchased from the upgrade shop, hold Space to fire them mid-flight for a burst of extra distance, best saved for after the initial ramp launch has already settled into a stable glide angle.

Coins earned from each attempt's total distance fund permanent upgrades to the ramp, glider, and rockets, so an early run's main purpose is banking coins for upgrades rather than achieving a personal-best distance on that specific attempt.

sections.heading: Glide angle is a constant tradeoff, not a set-and-forget input
sections.body: Holding the nose too high bleeds speed and stalls the glide early, while holding it too low dives into the water sooner than necessary. Making small corrections throughout the flight rather than picking one angle and holding it produces longer distances than either extreme.

sections.heading: Fire rockets after the glide stabilizes
sections.body: Because rockets add a burst of speed rather than lift, firing them immediately off the ramp before the penguin has settled into a stable glide angle can send the flight into an uncontrolled dive. Waiting until the glide is level before holding Space gets more usable distance out of the same rocket fuel.

sections.heading: Early runs are about coins, not distance records
sections.body: Since permanent upgrades to the ramp, glider, and rockets all come from coins earned by distance, treating the first several attempts as coin-farming runs rather than personal-best attempts builds toward genuinely longer flights faster than repeatedly trying to maximize an under-upgraded penguin's distance.

cut-the-rope.metaKeywords: Cut the Rope, cut the rope unblocked, zeptolab, om nom, physics puzzle game, schplay cut the rope
cut-the-rope.heroParagraph: Cut the Rope was released by ZeptoLab on October 4, 2010, and the goal in every level is the same: cut the ropes holding a piece of candy so it swings, falls, or bounces into the mouth of Om Nom, the small green creature waiting below, while collecting all three stars scattered along the way.
instructions: Click or swipe across a rope to cut it; the candy then swings or falls based on gravity and momentum, so cutting a rope at the wrong moment sends the candy in a direction that misses both the stars and Om Nom entirely.

Levels are grouped into boxes of 25, and each box introduces a new mechanic on top of the ones already learned — bubbles that float the candy upward, air cushions that bounce it, spikes that pop it instantly on contact — so a level pack later in the game combines mechanics rather than teaching them in isolation.

Collecting all three stars in a level is optional for finishing it but required in total count to unlock later boxes, so a level cleared by simply feeding Om Nom without the stars can still block progress if the box's star requirement is not met.

sections.heading: Order of cuts matters more than speed
sections.body: Because the candy's path depends on momentum built up from previous swings, cutting ropes in the wrong sequence can send it flying past a star or directly into a spike that a different cut order would have avoided entirely. Watching one full swing before committing to the next cut avoids compounding an early mistake.

sections.heading: Bubbles and cushions redirect, they don't just decorate
sections.body: A bubble carries the candy straight upward regardless of how it entered, and an air cushion bounces it in the direction the cushion is angled — both override the candy's existing momentum, so a rope cut that lines the candy up with a bubble or cushion is often more reliable than a direct swing toward Om Nom.

sections.heading: Star count gates progress, not just individual levels
sections.body: Since unlocking later boxes requires a minimum total star count rather than just clearing every level, skipping stars to rush through a box can leave you unable to access the next one even with every level technically completed. Replaying an early, easier level for its missed stars is often faster than struggling for stars on a harder one.

tanktrouble.heroParagraph: Tank Trouble is a maze tank shooter supporting 1-player (against the computer), 2-player, and 3-player local modes, where the defining mechanic is that every bullet bounces off walls instead of stopping — meaning a shot fired away from an opponent can still curve back around a corner and hit them.
instructions: In 2-player mode, Player 1 drives with the arrow keys and fires with M, while Player 2 drives with E, S, D, and F and fires with Q; 3-player mode keeps those two setups and adds a third player who drives and fires using only the mouse.

Every bullet bounces off maze walls rather than stopping on impact, so a shot that misses a direct line to an opponent can still ricochet through the maze and hit them a few walls later — firing down a corridor an opponent just left is often still worth it for the bounce.

Driving over certain pickups scattered through the maze upgrades your tank's firepower temporarily, so contesting a pickup near the center of the maze is often worth the risk of exposure it takes to reach it first.

sections.heading: Bounced shots are a real threat, not a miss
sections.body: Because bullets ricochet off walls instead of disappearing, an opponent hiding around a corner is not actually safe from a shot fired down the corridor they just occupied — accounting for bounce angles when firing, rather than only shooting at a direct line of sight, catches opponents who assume cover means safety.

sections.heading: Firepower pickups are worth contesting
sections.body: Since pickups scattered through the maze grant temporary weapon upgrades, driving toward one the instant it appears — even from a position that briefly exposes your tank — usually pays off more than playing purely defensively and letting an opponent claim every upgrade uncontested.

sections.heading: Maze layout dictates safe firing lines more than direct aim
sections.body: Because walls both block and redirect bullets, understanding a specific maze's corridor layout matters more for landing hits than raw aiming precision — a shot lined up correctly for a particular maze's geometry can hit an opponent who has no direct line of sight to you at all.

bad-icecream-1.heroParagraph: Bad Ice-Cream was made by Nitrome, casting an ice cream character that has to collect every piece of fruit scattered across each maze-like level while avoiding enemies, using ice blocks fired from its own mouth to trap threats or carve a safe path forward.

Press the action key to fire an ice block in the direction you are facing, which either blocks an enemy's path or builds a bridge across gaps; pressing it again on an existing block breaks that entire row or column of connected ice blocks at once.

Every piece of fruit in a level must be collected to clear it, so a level is not finished just by avoiding enemies — reaching fruit that requires building an ice bridge or trapping an enemy out of the way is often the actual obstacle, not survival alone.

sections.heading: Breaking ice clears a whole line, not one block
sections.body: Firing a second ice block into an already-placed one breaks the entire connected row or column at once rather than just that single block, which is useful both for freeing a path you sealed off by accident and for collapsing a wall of ice out from under a trapped enemy.

sections.heading: Ice blocks trap enemies, they don't damage them
sections.body: Since there is no direct attack on enemies, the only way to neutralize a threat is boxing it in with ice blocks so it cannot reach you while you collect nearby fruit — firing blocks reactively as an enemy approaches is less reliable than sealing off its path before it gets close.

sections.heading: Fruit placement, not enemy avoidance, decides most levels
sections.body: Because clearing a level requires collecting every piece of fruit rather than simply surviving, fruit placed across gaps or behind blocked paths is usually the real puzzle — building an ice bridge to reach isolated fruit matters as much as staying away from enemies.

crossyroad.heroParagraph: Crossy Road was developed by Hipster Whale, the indie studio of Andy Sun, Matt Hall, and Ben Weatherall, taking Frogger's road-crossing concept and rebuilding it as an endless, procedurally generated hopper where every run generates new lanes of traffic, water, and rail tracks.
instructions: Use the arrow keys or WASD to hop one lane at a time in any of four directions; each hop moves exactly one tile, so there is no partial movement or diagonal hopping between lanes.
Press Space to hop forward quickly in succession, useful for crossing a lane of fast-moving traffic where waiting for a full hop animation between presses would leave the character exposed too long.

Since the terrain is procedurally generated and different every run, memorizing a specific traffic pattern from a previous attempt does not transfer — each hop's timing has to be read from what is currently on screen rather than recalled from an earlier run.

sections.heading: Every hop is exactly one tile
sections.body: Because movement is locked to single-tile hops with no partial steps, positioning before a hop matters as much as the hop's direction — lining up with a safe gap one hop in advance is more reliable than hopping toward danger and correcting mid-lane, which is not possible once a hop is committed.

sections.heading: Rivers require riding logs, not swimming across
sections.body: Water lanes have no safe hop directly across them — the character can only cross by hopping onto floating logs or lily pads and riding them to the far bank, so treating a river lane the same as a road lane (hopping straight through) ends the run immediately.

sections.heading: Procedural generation means no memorized routes
sections.body: Since lane layouts regenerate every run, a route that worked on a previous attempt offers no guarantee on the next one — reading the current screen's traffic speed and gaps in real time is the only approach that scales as the game continues generating new terrain indefinitely.

ducklife2.heroParagraph: Duck Life 2 is Wix Games' sequel to the original training sim, adding a fourth minigame — Climbing — alongside the returning Running, Swimming, and Flying trials, all aimed at building stats before racing rival ducks for prize money.
instructions: Running trains speed: click to jump over obstacles like oranges, basketballs, watermelons, and baseballs that roll or bounce into your duck's path along the track.

sections.heading: Climbing rewards alternating rhythm, not one direction held
sections.body: Because the canyon requires jumping between two opposite walls rather than climbing straight up, holding one direction key without switching sends the duck straight into a wall instead of bouncing upward. Alternating left and right in rhythm with each landed jump is what actually gains height.

sections.heading: Obstacle variety in Running needs different reaction windows
sections.body: Since Running throws several different obstacle types — oranges, basketballs, watermelons, baseballs — with different sizes and bounce patterns, timing a jump for one obstacle type does not automatically transfer to the next; watching what is actually approaching matters more than reacting on a fixed rhythm.

sections.heading: Balance training across all four skills
sections.body: Because races test more than one stat at once, maxing out a single minigame like Flying while neglecting Climbing or Swimming leaves a duck that wins some races and loses others depending on the track. Spreading training sessions across all four minigames produces a more consistently competitive duck than specializing early.

duck-life-3.heroParagraph: Duck Life 3: Evolution, from Wix Games, adds a genetics layer on top of the training-and-racing formula: pick from four duck breeds with different starting strengths, then train until specific stat thresholds trigger a visible evolution into the next growth stage with a higher skill cap.
instructions: Running trains with the up arrow to jump over obstacles, Flying uses the left and right arrows to guide the duck's path, and Swimming combines the up arrow to jump, down arrow to dive, and left/right arrows to move — each minigame raises the matching stat used in races.

Reaching a stat threshold, such as level 20 in a given skill, triggers a visible evolution that raises the duck's skill cap for that stat, meaning further training past the old cap only becomes possible after the evolution actually happens.

Races are organized into three leagues — Amateur, Advanced, and Professional — set on the farm, in London, and on Easter Island respectively, with each league demanding higher stats than the last to be competitive.

A horizontal row that becomes completely filled across its width clears entirely, and everything above it shifts down to fill the gap — clearing multiple rows with a single piece placement scores more than clearing them one at a time across separate pieces.

The game ends when the stack of placed pieces reaches the top of the well, so leaving gaps or uneven surfaces that later pieces cannot fill cleanly is what typically causes the stack height to climb out of control rather than any single bad placement alone.

sections.heading: Clearing multiple rows at once is worth more than one at a time

sections.heading: Rotation should be planned before the piece reaches the stack

sections.heading: Payloads solve obstacles the original game had no answer for

sections.heading: Mode choice changes what actually counts as progress

sections.heading: Transmission has to outpace visibility

sections.heading: Resistances counter the response, not the population

sections.heading: The 8-ball is a hazard until your group is cleared

sections.heading: Power control matters as much as aim
sections.body: Because drag distance sets shot power directly, a well-aimed shot hit too hard can overshoot position for the next shot even while sinking the intended ball, so controlling power to leave the cue ball in a useful spot afterward is as important as sinking the current target.

snake.heroParagraph: This build is a browser recreation of Snake, the grid-based arcade concept most widely popularized by Nokia's mobile phones in the late 1990s, where a constantly growing line has to eat food without ever running into a wall or looping back into its own trailing body.

Eating a piece of food adds a segment to the snake's length and spawns a new piece of food elsewhere on the grid, so each successful bite makes the snake longer and correspondingly harder to maneuver through the same amount of space.

The run ends immediately the moment the snake's head touches a wall or any part of its own body, so a route that was safe when the snake was short can become a dead end once enough segments have been added.

sections.heading: Growth makes the same space progressively harder
sections.body: Because every piece of food eaten adds a permanent segment, a movement pattern that comfortably cleared the board early in a run can trap the snake against its own tail later on — planning routes with the snake's current length in mind, not just its length a few moves ago, avoids self-inflicted dead ends.

sections.heading: Turning early beats turning at the last moment
sections.body: Since the snake moves continuously and only changes direction on a keypress, waiting until the head is directly next to a wall or the snake's own body to turn leaves no margin for error — queuing a turn slightly before it is strictly necessary gives more room to correct if the turn does not clear the hazard as expected.

sections.heading: Open space should be preserved deliberately
sections.body: Because the snake's own body increasingly fills the available grid as it grows, deliberately looping through open areas rather than winding tightly back and forth keeps more usable space available for later in the run, when a longer snake needs more room to maneuver safely.

sections.heading: Upgrade categories interact, not just stack

spending-elonmusk-money.heroParagraph: Spend Elon's Money is a browser simulator built around a single goal: spend a virtual multi-billion-dollar fortune down to zero by buying items from a growing virtual marketplace, where each purchase unlocks access to new, often pricier things to spend on next.
instructions: Click Buy to purchase one unit of an item, or type in a specific quantity before clicking Buy to purchase several at once; click Sell to remove an item already added to your purchase list if you change your mind.
Each purchase can unlock new items in the marketplace that were not available before, so early spending decisions affect what becomes available to buy later, not just how much money remains.

Mixing small, cheap purchases with a few large ones tends to unlock more of the marketplace's variety than focusing purely on the most expensive items available, though going straight for big-ticket purchases drains the fortune fastest if speed is the goal.

sections.heading: Purchases unlock more of the marketplace, not just cost money
sections.body: Because buying certain items opens up new, often more expensive options that were not visible before, treating early purchases purely as a way to burn through cash misses that they also function as unlocks — a spending order that opens more categories early gives more to choose from for the rest of the run.

sections.heading: Speed and variety pull in opposite directions
sections.body: Since focusing entirely on the most expensive available items drains the fortune fastest, while mixing categories and price points unlocks and shows off more of what the marketplace actually offers, the choice between rushing to zero and exploring everything available is a real tradeoff rather than one clearly better approach.

sections.heading: Sell lets you correct a purchase without restarting
sections.body: Because the Sell button removes an item already added to the purchase list, changing your mind about a specific buy does not require restarting the whole session — using Sell to adjust a spending plan partway through is a normal part of managing the run rather than a sign something went wrong.

shuffle.metaKeywords: Shuffle, shuffle unblocked, shockwave games, marble knockout game, curling billiards hybrid, schplay shuffle
shuffle.heroParagraph: Shuffle is a 1999 Shockwave.com game blending curling, marbles, and billiards: you control a row of red marbles and have to knock every yellow marble off the board before the computer manages to knock all of yours off first, with rebound physics off the board's edges playing a central role in how shots actually land.
instructions: Click one of your red marbles and drag the mouse to set both the throwing angle and the power behind the shot; release the mouse button to launch it toward the yellow marbles.
Clearing every yellow marble off the board before the computer clears all of your red ones advances you to the next level, which then gives you fewer marbles to work with than the level before.
Rebound physics off the board's edges let a single well-aimed shot bank off a corner and take out multiple yellow marbles in one throw, rather than needing a separate shot for each one.

sections.heading: Bank shots multiply the value of a single throw
sections.body: Because rebounding off a corner or edge can redirect a marble into a second or third yellow target after the initial hit, lining up a bank shot that clears several yellows at once is far more efficient than aiming directly at one yellow marble per throw, especially as levels give fewer marbles to work with.

sections.heading: Throw strength needs calibration, not just aim
sections.body: Since overshooting sends your own marble past the target (and potentially off the board, wasting it), tweaking throw strength to match the actual distance to a target — rather than always throwing at maximum power — avoids losing marbles to overshoot, which matters more as later levels give fewer marbles to spare.

sections.heading: Fewer marbles per level raises the cost of a wasted shot
sections.body: Because clearing a level reduces the marble count for the next one, a throw that misses or overshoots becomes proportionally more costly on later levels than it was early on — later levels reward more deliberate aiming and power control than the more forgiving early levels required.

sections.heading: This is a full continuation, not a single boss fight

sections.heading: The premise shapes what to expect from encounters
sections.body: Because the story follows a timeline already corrupted by repeated failed resets, characters and battles reflect that history rather than behaving like a first playthrough of the original game — prior expectations from a normal Undertale run may not hold in this specific continuation.

sections.heading: Bullet-hell fundamentals still apply

sections.heading: Each phase adds patterns rather than replacing them
sections.body: Because this is a three-phase escalating fight, patterns introduced in an earlier phase often continue to appear alongside new ones in later phases — a pattern learned early stays relevant throughout the fight rather than becoming obsolete once a new phase begins.

sections.heading: Y Blasters demand precise lateral positioning, not just movement
sections.body: Since the Y Blaster attack fires three Gaster Blaster beams in a spread formation, standing in a position that dodges one beam does not necessarily clear the other two — finding the specific gap between all three beams is required rather than reacting to just the nearest one.

sections.heading: Simultaneous bone spawns from both ends require full-corridor awareness
sections.body: Because Back and Forth Bones spawns sliders from both ends of the corridor at the same time, focusing only on one direction misses the threat approaching from the other side — tracking both ends of the play space at once is necessary rather than watching a single direction.
